4. Briefly stated, plaintiff-appellants claimed that Salimabad hat as now exists in the plots mentioned in the schedule to the plaint namely, CS plot Nos. 426,427 and 428 of mouza Salimabad, PS Nagarpur, Tangail was established long before 1850 AD. It used to sit twice a week, namely, on Tuesdays and Fridays. As the site of this hat was washed away by the river Jamuna it was shifted to village Binanoo within PS Pakulla and sat on Tuesdays and Fridays. After Binanoo was also washed away by the same river the hat was shifted to Tabaria and continued to sit there under the name and style of "Salimabad Hat" on Tuesdays and Fridays. When the old site on which Salimabad hat used to sit reappeared it was shifted from Tabaria to its present site it mouza Salimabad. Since its shifting there Salimabad hat is being held on Tuesdays and Fridays. The shifting occurred during SA operation (from the year 1957 to 1963). After emergence of Bangladesh some interested persons started a hat at Tabaria, which also began to sit on Tuesdays and Fridays. 

 This is to report that I enquired into the matter locally on 25-4-71 after notification of both the parties. I visited the new established bazaar at Salimabad mouza and also the old established hat at Tabaria mouza and talked to the members of public of both the parties. It appears to me that the new bazaar established at Salimabad mouza is at a distance of 1/3rd of a mile from the old hat of Tabaria mouza. The old hat having its long standing tradition and history is known publicly as Salimabad Tabaria bazaar and is beneficial to thousands of people surrounding it. All the Government local offices are situated within the vicinity of the old hat including a High School of course, the old hat is now congested and demands extension and there are lands also for its extension. As regards the new bazaar at Salimabad mouza, the reason of establishing another bazaar within short distance of an old hat and bazaar, they explained to me that the new bazaar is just an extension of the old one. The people of Salimabad mouza also clearly stated to me that the old hat is just adjacent to their mouza and they can derive all sorts of facilities from the old one as hat and bazaar. From my physical enquiry of the new bazaar it appears that the bazaar has been started from January 1971 wherein 10 shops running and 13 more structures are going to be raised shortly under the super- vision of a Committee led by Mr Akramuzzaman as its Chairman. From my query the members of the new bazaar committee told me that they did not seek permission from appropriate authority concerned for establishing the bazaar. 

 On the other hand the case of the Opposite party i.e. the people behind Tabaria hat is that the Tabaria hat has been actually functioning for a long time and it was Salimabad hat, which was set up by some interested people after liberation with the same hat days as those of the Tabaria Hat. The local Administration after making enquiries came to the decision Salimabad hat was not in existence from the time of wholesale acquisition. It was established in 1971 on some private lands. The local administration therefore forfeited the lands and buildings of the hat and took over possession of the hat. They, however, decided to allow the hat to function on Wednesday and Sunday to avoid Clash with the Tabaria hat, which had been functioning on Tuesday and Friday. As regards the Tabaria hat, the local administration found that it was in existence at the time of wholesale acquisition and taking over of the possession of the Tabaria hat had been delayed for delay in the preparation of CA Rolls, which was in progress. 

 I do not find it necessary to go into details of the question as to which hat is older. The facts that the CA Rolls of the Tabaria hat is under preparation, if establishes that the Tabaria hat was in existence at the time of wholesale acquisition. The fact that the Salimabad hat is situated on tenanted lands, which have not been acquired as lands of hat, also proves that it was not in existence at the time of wholesale acquisition. Moreover, enquiries made by the local administration established beyond reasonable doubt that the Salimabad hat was established in 1971. The lands and buildings of the Salimabad hat have, therefore, been rightly forfeited to Govt. The hat could also be closed down. This has not been done; it has been allowed to function under the management of the Government. Now the only question to decide is on which days the two hats should function. Since the two hats are situated quite closely it is neither desirable nor justified that the hats should sit on the same days. It is only natural that the two hats should sit on different days. Since the Tabaria hat has been sitting on Tuesday and Friday there is no reason to change its days. Since Salimabad hat is a new hat and has been allowed to continue, fixation of its hat days on Wednesday and Sunday is reasonable and rational. If the persons concerned are interested in the functioning of the Salimabad hat, they should abide by the decision taken by the local administration and upheld by Government if they continued to flout the Government decision, there is no alternative but to close down the Salimabad hat as decided by Government. In view of the facts discussed above, the petition is rejected and the order to maintain status quo is vacated. 

 10. Being aggrieved appellants filed the aforesaid suit, Defendant No.7 Golam Hossain Khan contested the aforesaid suit by filing two separate written statements, contesting inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and that the Tabaria hat being older and originally known as "Chandganj Hat" used to sit on Tuesday and Friday and that Salimabad hat which is a new hat cannot be allowed to sit for the same days, that is Tuesday and Friday and as it would derogate from the privilege of the people of the locality. Mention was also made of all the orders passed by the Government as mentioned above. It was also mentioned that plaintiff No. 7, filed OC Suit No. 94 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Tangail and obtained an order of ad interim injunction against the order of the ADC dated 8-3-77, which was vacated by the order, dated 24-2-78. Secretary, Salimabad Hat Committee filed Civil Revision Nos. 368 and 372 of 1978 before the High Court Division Writ Petition No. 442 of 1978 challenging the order dated 24-2-78 and the aforesaid civil revision cases were heard analogously by a Bench of the High Court Division which discharged the Rules. 

 13. In brief, his findings were that one of the important ingredients as appears in the definition of a hat in section 2(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is the place upon which it sits and, if the hat shifts to a new place though it may continue ill the same name for all practical purposes it is a new hat; that plaintiff appellants had no customary right by immemorial user in respect of Salimabad hat and even if it had such right it came to an end on the vesting of the hat in the Government under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act; that in the absence of any provisions of law and any right of immemorial user, the order passed by the Joint Secretary, Government of Bangladesh on 8-3-77 could not be questioned in Civil Court; that the order of the Joint Secretary is not malafide or arbitrary as he appears to have sufficient materials for arriving at the conclusion; that Civil Court could only enquire whether the order of the Joint Secretary was malafide or arbitrary or was based on sufficient materials and it did not fall within the domain of the Civil Court to embark upon an independent inquiry to determine which hat was older; that Civil Court should not have, therefore, declared the order dated 4-4-78 illegal, void and not binding upon Salimabad hat; that since the order of forfeiture of Salimabad hat was not acted upon and Salimabad hat was allowed to sit on two days in a week other than Tuesday and Friday, plaintiff appellants had no cause of action in respect of the order dated 24- 2-78, Exhibit A(2); and that since plaintiff appellants claimed no right in respect of the Tabaria Hat, no declaration could be given that Tabaria hat was a new hat and was liable to be closed down. 

 16. Mr KA Bakr, Attorney-General, who appeared for respondent No. 1, submitted that the appellants' claim as regards franchise of a market has no legs to stand upon. Franchise of a market as claimed in the present case meant the right to hold Salimabad hat at its present site in Salimabad Mouza on two days in a week, Tuesday and Friday. The claim is not tenable for two reasons, first, no grant either by the Government or any local body to hold Salimabad hat at any point of time has been established and secondly, plaintiff appellants have been unable to show that in the absence of such grant they acquired the franchise by prescription, the establishment of Salimabad hat being quite recent. Even conceding that such franchise was at all granted by the Government, such franchise has been lost due to the erosion of the place where Salimabad hat is claimed to have existed around 1850 AD. It did not travel from place to place till Salimabad hat came to Tabaria. Also, the learned Attorney- General denied most emphatically the existence of franchise in the sub-continent of which this country is a part. In support of his contention, he cited a few decisions, which shall be presently considered by us. Since the franchise of a market is not recognized by or under any law in force in this country, appellants cannot get such declaration from the Court. Attorney-General Bakr next submitted that it is the Government alone which possesses the power to grant franchise of a hat as provided in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Ordinance XIX of 1959 and therefore, it is the government alone which has the right to fix the date or dates on which a hat is to sit. On which day or days a hat will sit cannot, therefore, be declared by any Court. In this connection he also submitted that in view of the publication of the compensation assessment roll in the notification dated 11th April 1978 published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 20th April 1978, no right in relation to Salimabad hat can any longer be claimed by the appellants. These considerations apart, on proper inquiries Government arrived at the decision whose validity has been challenged before the Court. There has been no impropriety either in ordering the inquiries or in conducting the same. 

 18. Turning to the definition of hat as provided in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, appellants" Counsel submitted that the learned Judge of the High Court Division in attaching undue importance to 'place' being the sole element in the definition lost sight of one of the most essential elements of a 'hat' which is the sitting days in a week on which a hat assembles. Apart from showing the ancientness of the Salimabad hat from these documents, the Counsel also tried to establish therefrom the sitting of Salimabad hat on Tuesday and Friday in a week from the very beginning. 

 22. Firstly, with reference to the definition of 'hat' as provided in section 2(12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, he submitted that it does not merely mean the name it bears or the place where it is held. A hat connotes each and every element included in the definition. He therefore, most emphatically asserted that Salimabad hat which is claimed to have existed for more than a century and a half from now somewhere other than at Tabaria or its present site cannot be impugned to have continued since then with all its rights including its oldness and sitting days in a week. He regretted that the trial Court and the first appellate Court proceeded on a wrong assumption and held that Salimabad hat was carrying with it all its supposed rights to which ever place it has been moving since 1850 AD. Besides, they did not properly consider the evidence in arriving at their decision that Salimabad hat was older among the two hats, Salimabad and Tabaria, counsel also mentioned that there was no compensation assessment roll in respect of the plots upon which Salimabad hat now sits, Further, those plots are now recorded in the names of private individuals. There is no mention of the existence of any hat on them. This has also been admitted in the plaint. PWs 1 to 3 also admitted the establishment of Salimabad hat on its present site only 15 or 16 years ago. On the other hand, the existence of Tabaria hat is proved from the evidence, such as Exhibit 2, Exhibit 'E' Government notification dated 11-4-78 published in the compensation assessment Roll. 

 23. He also submitted that having regard to the provisions of section 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the correctness of the compensation assessment roll can no longer be challenged in the present case and the Civil Court has no jurisdiction to determine whether Tabaria hat is a new hat, or to put it differently, Salimabad is older than Tabaria hat. 

 31. Vigorous attempts have been made by Counsels of both parties to present correct views on what are the constituent elements of a 'hat' and are also what is meant by franchise of a market or 'hat'. For this purpose, reference was made to cases dealing with the statutory definition of hat as provided in section 2 (12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as already mentioned above. Section 2 (12) defines a hat as follows: 

 "the market was a market without metes and bounds and might extend, therefore, from time to time as the crowded state of the market might require over any of these surrounding streets, all of which were to be presumed to have been dedicated to the public subject to the exercise of the market franchise notwithstanding the Paving Acts as such Acts were not to be construed as interfering with the market rights." 

 (7) In the United States, a franchise is a privilege of a public nature conferred by a legislative grant (State vs Weatherly, 45 No. 20). 

 "The first point is the somewhat shadowy claim set up by the plaintiff, that his hat is a very ancient hat and that, on that ground, he is entitled to some special protection, it is true that the hat has existed for a considerable time and it also appears that it is shown on the revenue survey map with the date 1926 below it. Beyond that however there are no materials which carry the history of the hat back to the permanent settlement and the Subordinate Judge has found that the evidence does not establish that is existed and that the hat was in existence in 1793, the case of Rakhal Das Addy vs Durga Sundari Dasi would be a complete answer to the plaintiff's claim. In this part of India, there appears to be no such thing as a market franchise or a right to hold a market conferred by grant from the Crown. At any rate, so far as we are aware and as the learned vakil for the plaintiff has been able to information us, there is no authority which affirms the existence of such a right and no authority which countenances the acquisition of any such right by prescription." 

 47. In observing that in England no one can hold a market without a licence from the Crown, the learned Judges did not fail to mention the reason for this, as has been stated in an English decision: 

 57. Dr Hossain, next referred to the case of Secretary of State vs Tameside, (1976) 3 All ER. 665. In this case, the responsibility for providing public education was distributed under the Education Act. 1944 between the Secretary of State and local education authority. The Act conferred upon the local education authorities a broad discretion to choose what are the best means for providing the variety of instruction in their respective areas. A newly-elected council in Tameside had two courses open to it, one was to make entry to all the secondary schools non-selective, the other was to leave the character of all the secondary schools in the area the same as in the previous year, i.e. that selective entry to the five grammar schools and non-selective entry to the remaining schools. The right to choose between the courses was prima facie that of the council alone. Under section 68 of the Act the Secretary of State had the power to over-rule their choice if he had satisfied him- self that the council purported to act 'unreasonably'. In stating that in public law 'unreasonably' as descriptive of the way in which a public authority exercises a discretion vested in it by law has become a "term of legal art, the Judicial Committee of the House of Lords were of the view that the conduct of a public authority becomes unreasonable when it is seen that no sensible authority acting with due appreciation of its responsibilities would have decided to adopt. Lord Diplock observed: 

 "The very concept of administrative discretion involves a right to choose between more than one possible course of action on which there is room for reasonable people to hold differing opinions as to which is to be preferred. It has from beginning to end of these proceedings been properly conceded by Counsel for the Secretary of State that his own strong preference and that of the Government of which he is a member for non-selective entry to all secondary schools, is not of itself a ground on which he could be satisfied that the council would be acting unreasonably if they gave effect to their contrary preference for the retention of selective entry to the five grammar proposed to give effect to that preference would in the light of the circumstances as they existed on 11 June 1976, involve such interference with the provision of efficient instruction and training in secondary schools in their area that no sensible authority acting with due appreciation of their responsibilities under the act could have decided to adopt the course which the council were then proposing" 

 ''It was for the Secretary of State to decide that it is not for any Court of law to substitute its own opinion for his, but it is for a Court of law to determine whether it has been established that in reaching his decision unfavourable to the council he had directed himself properly in law and had in consequence taken into consideration the matters which on the true construction of the Act he ought to have considered and excluded from his consideration, matters that were irrelevant to what he had to consider." 

 58. Facts of this case, being different in complexion and nature, executive discretion as determined by the committee will be found to have no scope for application in the case before us. The question before the Judicial Committee was whether the directive of the Secretary of State requiring the authority to act in a certain manner was legal. The Court was to judge whether his judgment of the authority's action has been proper or not. The committee in saying that it was not the Court's duty to substitute its own views for those of the Secretary of State, Lord Diplock observed: 

 59. "The task of the Court, in the present circumstances, is to decide whether there was any foundation of fact on which the Secretary of State could properly come to the conclusion on 11th June 1976 that the authority had acted as no reasonable local authority could have acted in refusing to implement the comprehensive scheme. If there was such a foundation, then he was entitled to issue the directive even though the Court may differ from his view." 

 60. Since, after the acquisition on hats and bazaars by the Government it has become the sole authority to control, establish and regulate hats and bazaars, the discretion of the Government to fix days on which a particular hat is to sit cannot be interfered with by anybody else. The contention between the two hats is over the sitting days of the respective hats. If after making inquiry and local inspection, the Government has fixed the days, Court has no authority to alter them on the ground that the Government decision has been arbitrary or illegal. 

 61. On the failure of the appellants to establish their right of franchise, either by grant or by prescription, in respect of Salimabad hat, there seems to be no reason to say that the Government unjustly or even unjustifiably interfered with the sitting days of Salimabad hat. Some papers were, however, produced to show the existence of Salimabad hat from 1850 AD but as already observed they are not sufficient to establish either its antiquity or its continuity, though verbally assertions have been made about its ancient original and movements from place to place. Even conceding the appellants claim as to its oldness no link has been established between such hats as assembled at Salimabad, Binanoo, Tabaria and then lastly to Salimabad. Nothing has been produced to show what rights Salimabad possessed or exercised or who exercised them on its-behalf as it kept moving from place to place. Further, after the acquisition of all hats and bazaars no individual or individuals could claim an inherent right to exercise rights relating to them, which are not conferred upon them under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. So far as the claim to sit on Tuesday and Friday is concerned, appellant's rights approached the Government to fix them accordingly, but having been unable to convince the authority of the rightness of their claim civil Court was approached to determine the same. Learned arguments were advanced by the Counsel of the parties to substantiate their respective claims as to the existence or non-existence of the franchise of a market. It appears on consideration of the laws relating to that such right has not been recognized in our law beginning from either before the creation, or emergence of this country. In these circumstances the appellants attempt to establish their right of franchise of a market in the Civil Court would appear to be vain and futile. 

 For the reasons stated above, the appeals are dismissed. There would, however, be no order as to costs. 

 65. The defendant Nos. 2 and 7 contested the suit by filing written statement. Their case was that Tabaria hat is an old hat and used to sit regularly on Tuesday and Friday for more than 100 years. That Salimabad hat and Tabaria hat are adjacent to each other. The SA record shows the existence of Tabaria hat. 

 67. Defendants filed (a) copy of the order dated 14-11-1972 passed by the Deputy Commissioner, Tangail marked Exhibit A (3), (b) certified copies of the new SA Khatian Nos. 45/74/83/16/23/32/140/150/151/152 of Mouza Tabaria market Exhibit B and (c) certified copies of the SA Khatian Nos. 246/897/ 736/603/939 of Salimabad Mouza market Exhibit C series, (d) a map prepared in 1972 under the authority of Surveyor-General of Bangladesh (e) a RS Map of Mouza Tabaria prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act marked Exhibits D and D (1), (f) registered Saf-kabala dated 9-4-59 AD and Saf-kabala dated 19-10-53 marked Exhibits E and E (1), (g) certified copy of the order passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 442 of 1978 and Civil Revision No. 368 of 1978 marked Exhibits F, (h) certified copies of the judgment of temporary injunction passed on 29-7-1977 by the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Tangail and (i) a certified copy of the judgment of Miscellaneous appeal Nos. 61 and 62 of 1977 passed on 31-1-1978 by the District Judge, Tangail marked Exhibit G series. 

 74. The matter came before the High Court Division in Revision. The learned Single Judge considered the definition of "Hat and Bazar" in section 2 (12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and took the view that the place where a hat sits is very important ingredient of the definition of a hat and if the site of a hat is shifted from one place to another, the hat in the new place though called by the same is in fact in law a new hat distinct and separate from the hat at the old place." It was found that the customary right as claimed by the plaintiffs having the hat days on Tuesdays and Fridays will also be an 'encumbrance' within the meaning of section 3 (2) of the Act and relying on a decision reported in 10 DLR 523, it was held that the customary right by immemorial user, was wiped out on the vesting of the hat in the Government free from encumbrances. The learned Single Judge then considered that in the absence of any wrong done to the plaintiffs in the enjoyment of the hat, they cannot feel aggrieved. Further, it was found the order of the Joint Secretary dated 8-3-77 could not be challenged before the Civil Court and observed that "the Joint Secretary had applied his judicial order (viewed) and as such an order can hardly be called in question as malafide and arbitrary". It was observed: 

 87. In 10 DLR 523 the learned Single Judge considered the question whether the Hindu residents of the locality who used to celebrate Durga Puja, Lakshmi Puja and Kali Puja on the land from time immemorial could claim their customary right to use the suit land as a place of worship. After the acquisition of the estate itself under the State Acquisition Tenancy Act, the learned Single Judge considered it an "encumbrance" within the meaning of section 2, Clause 10 and accordingly held: that there was no basis of the suit which therefore was dismissed for want of cause of auction. 

 Definition of hat or bazaar under section 2 (12) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was considered and the learned Single Judge concluded: 

 That there must be place is so obvious because it cannot exist in vacuum. It is not the question on which particular part of land, the hat or bazaar sits, the question is the date of assembly itself of that hat. It is linked with economic necessity of the locality and a hat or bazaar determines the economic relationship of the society of which it is an integral part. As opposed to bazaar, a hat is held only on certain days. Mr FA Sachse ICS in his final report on the survey and settlement operations in Mymensingh District Stated in 1920. 

 92. Even the Government Manual says "hats and markets may be established in Government estates where there is demand for these to suit the convenience of Khas Mahal tenants. When there are suitable hats in existence for a long time in the neighbourhood, there is no need to establish a new one in the Khas Mahal." 

 It has argued that with the acquisition of the estates the encumbrances have been wiped out. The definition of encumbrance is as under: 

 "2(10) .... "Encumbrance", in relation to any estate, tenure, holding, tenancy or land, means any mortgage, charge, lien, sub-tenancy, easement or other right or interest created by the holder thereof on such estate, tenure, holding, tenancy or land or in limitation of his own interest therein." 

 97 A. In the definition of encumbrance the words "easement or other right or interest" are to be understood in ejusdom generis that the general words will be restricted to things of the same nature as those which have been already mentioned. To put it simply if a general words is added to specific words, the general word would take its colour from the specific words, therefore the words 'other right of interest' are to be understood in the light of easement but the customary right stands on a different footing. During the last one hundred years the customary law determining economic necessity were not disturbed and neither the Bengal Tenancy Act nor the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act contemplated any such right as 'encumbrance.' A customary right determining the economic factors operating in social life cannot be treated as encumbrance. To hold otherwise is to say that man exists for a technical rule. 

 98. It is the customary right that was infringed by an executive action. The plaintiff brought the suit as he was aggrieved. The learned Single Judge unfortunately could not appreciate the grievance of plaintiffs. Further the reasoning of the High Court Division is fallacious and fraught with self-evident contradiction. If Salimabad hat is a new hat it comes within the mischief of law. Instead Salimabad hat was allowed to sit on some other day but not Tuesday or Friday. Here is the inconsistency if it is to sit it must sit on Tuesday and Friday because the concurrent finding of fact is that notwithstanding the shifting of the hat from place to place due to erosion the hat used to sit on those two particular days-Tuesday and Friday. A rival group of people took advantage of the shifting of Salimabad to Tabaria mouza and when Salimabad came back to its own original place, they set up a hat called Tabaria hat, which concurrently was found to be a new hat. The local revenue authorities favoured Tabaria and a new tussle started between the two hats. Government failed to tackle the issue keeping in view the economic necessity of the locality after all, market is determined by the laws of economies, instead the Government allowed both the hats to operate-significantly allowing Tabaria to sit on Tuesday and Friday although it was the claim of Salimabad, not only a rival market was created but by changing the date of assembly an unjust situation was created for the redress of which the plaintiff brought the suit. The suit was decreed on contest. It was affirmed by the Appellate Court. The High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction disturbed the finding of fact since "There are errors apparent on the face of the record". The concurrent finding of fact was upset in the revisional jurisdiction. Rule as to concurrent finding of fact is not so rigid that it might not be departed from if such a state of things existed as facts appearing from some undisputed document, which are completely destructive of the finding of fact, by the Courts below. AIR 1941 PC 55, AIR 1947 PC 19, 28 CLJ73 BC. 63, CLJ 410 Pc. That was not the case here. It is not the error of fact but the error of law, which is the requirement of law that calls for exercise of jurisdiction. The High Court Division further went to the length of saying that the decision of the local authorities cannot be challenged in a Civil Court without giving any reasons although reliance was placed on two decisions none of which as discussed earlier, have any manner of application.
